chunks: "I'd design it for a 48 volt bus, a 5 amp motor and a 3. 3 volt microcontroller. The PFET has its source on the bus and its drain to the motor.
It needs to be off with the gate at the bus voltage and on with the gate about 12 volts below it. I'll use a small N-channel FET as the level shifter.
Its source is at ground, so the GPIO can drive its gate through 220 ohms with a 100 k pulldown, like any low-side switch.
Its drain connects through a 10 kilohm resistor to the PFET's gate node.
A second resistor, also 10 k, pulls the gate up to the bus, which holds the PFET off whenever the shifter is off or unpowered.
And a 12 volt Zener from gate to source clamps V GS so the gate can never be pulled more than 12 volts below the source, even at 60 volts.
When the GPIO goes high, the shifter turns on and pulls the gate node toward ground through the 10 k, but the Zener stops it at the bus minus 12 volts, so V GS is minus 12 and the PFET is fully on.
The current in that path is about 3. 6 milliamps at 48 volts, about 130 milliwatts in the resistor, so I'd use a half-watt part.
The shifter needs to be rated above the bus: a 100 volt part. When the GPIO goes low the pull-up recharges the gate.
The limit is speed: 10 k with a 2 nanofarad gate is a 20 microsecond time constant, with a plateau of a few microseconds at 5 amps and 48 volts, so about 0.
5 millijoule per edge: fine at 100 hertz to 1 kilohertz, a problem above that. For faster PWM I'd add a push-pull stage, or switch to an NFET with a bootstrap driver."
